Power washing in Dallas is not a luxury chore here. North Texas gives the outside of a house a hard year: oak pollen that turns a car yellow in spring, hail and wind-driven dirt from spring storms, months of heat, and shade that keeps the north wall green. This free line connects you with a local company that cleans it properly.

Dallas Power Washing Pro is a phone line and this website, nothing more. It does not own a pressure washer and never sends anyone out. When you call, an automated assistant answers, asks what you need cleaned and roughly how big it is, and transfers you to an independent, locally owned pressure washing company in the Dallas-Fort Worth area. That company comes out, gives you its own price, does the work and is paid by you. If it cannot pick up, your name, number, city and job are passed along so it can call you back.

Pressure washing in Dallas: why the method matters more than the machine

Anyone can rent a pressure washer. The difference between a good result and a damaged surface is knowing when not to use full pressure. The groups that write the care rules for building materials are blunt about it:

  • Brick: the Brick Industry Association warns that excessive pressure can damage brick faces and erode mortar joints, and that high-pressure water cleaning "is not appropriate for brick." Brick is everywhere in DFW, so this matters on almost every house.
  • Shingle roofs: the Asphalt Roofing Manufacturers Association says not to use a power washer on a roof at all, because high pressure is likely to damage asphalt roofing. Black streaks are algae, and they come off with a soft wash.
  • Composite decks: Trex allows a gentle pressure wash on its newer boards only within its own limits and spray distance, and says going past them can void the warranty.

So the useful question when you talk to a company is not "how strong is your machine," it is "how will you clean each surface." The line connects you with a company that can answer that.

What North Texas weather does to the outside of a home

DFW averages about 37 inches of rain a year, according to the National Weather Service's 1991 to 2020 normals, but it rarely comes gently. Spring storms bring hail, and the Insurance Council of Texas has counted Tarrant County as the most hail-struck county in the state. After a storm, siding and walks carry a film of grit and torn leaves.

Summer is the opposite problem. The Weather Service says DFW's first 100 degree day arrives on average around July 1 and the last around August 27, and 2011 had a record 71 of them. Heat bakes dirt onto concrete and fades a fence fast. Winter can freeze hard too: in February 2021 DFW Airport hit 2 degrees below zero and stayed at or below freezing for 139 hours straight, which is why a careful company will not wash on a day that is about to freeze.

Then there is the shade. The north side of a house, the strip under a live oak and the fence behind a hedge stay damp longest, and that is where green and black growth starts. A good wash treats that growth so it does not come straight back.

Before anyone sprays: four things to ask any company

Proof of liability insurance

Texas has no state license for pressure washing, so insurance is the real protection if a window breaks or water gets into a wall. Ask to see the certificate.

A written price for each surface

House, driveway, fence and roof priced separately, so you can compare quotes line by line and nothing changes once the work starts.

Soft wash for siding, roofs and wood

Ask which surfaces get low pressure and a cleaning solution, and which get a surface cleaner. "We just blast it" is the wrong answer for brick, shingles and cedar.

Where the wash water goes

Dallas says letting soapy wash water reach a storm drain violates city code, and Fort Worth bans wash water in its storm drains. A good company blocks the drain and plans for runoff. See the Texas rules guide.

Common questions

Who does power washing in Dallas?

Hundreds of small, locally owned companies, from one-truck operators to firms with several crews. This line does not do the work. It answers your call, asks what needs cleaning, and transfers you to one independent DFW company, which inspects the job, quotes it and does it. You can still get other quotes; nothing about the call commits you.

Is pressure washing the same as power washing?

Close, but not quite. Both use a machine to push water hard at a surface. Power washing usually means the water is heated, which helps on grease and oil, and it generally costs more. Pressure washing usually means cold water. Siding, roofs and wood are a third case, called soft washing, where pressure stays low and a cleaning solution does most of the work. The power vs pressure washing guide goes into detail.

How much does pressure washing cost in Dallas?

It depends on the surface, the size and how dirty it is, and only the company that sees the job can quote it. For a rough national picture, Angi's October 2026 cost guide puts most whole-house jobs between $213 and $449 and most driveways between $100 and $250. The DFW cost guide has the full ranges and what pushes a price up.

Does calling the line cost anything?

No. The call and the connection are free, and the line never bills you. The pressure washing company you are connected with quotes its own price and is paid by you directly. Companies may pay the line a referral fee, which is how it stays free.

Which cities around Dallas does the line cover?

Dallas and the Dallas-Fort Worth area, including Fort Worth, Arlington, Plano, Frisco, McKinney, Allen, Denton, Irving, Carrollton, Addison and Flower Mound. Each has its own page under service areas with the local rules worth knowing before anyone sprays a driveway.
